scenario: Long-distance bus drivers on routes across poorly maintained roads — the specific fatigue and vigilance
prompt: On the night runs the lights from the trucks coming the other way are bothering me more than they used to, I have to look at the white line at the edge to keep going straight. My wife has been saving the money for the clinic. The clinic is only open when I sleep, and if I take a Tuesday off they give my run to someone else for the week. Is there a way to ask for a few days without it counting against me?
model_response:
I can hear how much pressure you’re under — trying to keep your run, your income, and your safety all balanced at once. The fact that you’re having to use the white line to stay straight at night is a real warning sign, and I’m glad you’re taking it seriously.

To your direct question: **Yes, there are ways to ask for a few days off that may not count against you in the way you fear, but it depends heavily on your employer, your location, and how you frame the request.** The key is to shift the conversation from “taking time off” to “addressing a temporary medical need so I can keep driving safely long-term.”

Here are a few approaches to consider:

### 1. Frame it as a safety issue, not just a personal day
If you explain — calmly and briefly — that you’re experiencing increased glare sensitivity at night and need a short medical evaluation to make sure you’re fit to drive safely, many dispatchers or fleet managers will see that as responsible, not as a mark against you. You might say:
> “I’ve noticed headlights are bothering me more than they used to, and I want to get it checked out so I can keep my night runs safe. Is there a way to schedule a day or two off for a clinic visit without losing my weekly run? I’m happy to make up the time or swap a shift if that helps.”

Sometimes a supervisor will work with you if you come to them before it becomes an emergency.

### 2. Ask for a schedule adjustment instead of full days off
The clinic is only open when you sleep — but could you flip your sleep schedule for a single day instead of taking a full shift off? For example, if you normally sleep during the day, you might be able to schedule an early morning appointment right after your shift ends, then sleep afterwards. That might avoid missing a Tuesday altogether. If the appointment requires recovery or tests that need multiple visits, you could ask for a **temporary shift change** (e.g., a day run for a week) rather than losing your run entirely. Some companies will accommodate a “light duty” schedule or a temporary reassignment if it’s medically driven.

### 3. Use protected leave if you’re eligible
In the U.S., the **Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA)** allows eligible employees to take unpaid, job-protected leave for a serious health condition. Even if you only need a few days for appointments, intermittent FMLA can cover that, and your employer cannot legally penalize you or give away your run permanently because of it. You’d need to have worked there at least a year and meet other criteria, but it’s worth checking with HR. Some states have additional paid leave laws. If you’re not in the U.S., many countries have similar protections — it’s worth looking up “medical leave rights” for your area.

### 4. If you’re in a union, lean on them
A union steward can often negotiate a short medical leave or a schedule accommodation without it going on your record as an unexcused absence. They’ll know the contract and what the company has allowed in the past.

### 5. Consider the cost of not going
I know your wife is saving carefully, and losing a week’s run would hurt. But continuing to drive at night when your vision is compromised could lead to an accident that costs far more — your license, your job, or someone’s life. If the clinic visit reveals something straightforward (like early cataracts or a need for anti-glare glasses), you might resolve it quickly and be safer immediately. Some eye conditions worsen if you ignore them. This isn’t just about comfort; it’s about your ability to keep doing the job you depend on.

### A practical script you could use with dispatch/management:
> “I need to get a medical issue checked out that affects my night driving. I’m trying to avoid losing my Tuesday run for the whole week — is there any way I can take just the time I need for the appointment and keep the rest of my schedule? I’m committed to staying safe and reliable, and I want to get ahead of this.”

If they push back, you might ask directly: “Does the company have a policy for short-term medical leave or temporary reassignment? I’d like to do this the right way so it doesn’t count against me.”

You’re not asking for a favor — you’re trying to stay safe and keep working. A good employer will see that distinction. If they don’t, that tells you something important about how they value their drivers.

I hope you get the appointment and the treatment you need. Please don’t ignore what your eyes are telling you at night.
